title: Alex Chesterman's Smaller Plan for Cazoo, and the Collapse After It
dek: In January 2023 Cazoo's founder cut its targets and stepped aside as chief executive; sixteen months later the car retailer was in administration.

story.event: Resetting Cazoo's plan and stepping aside as chief executive before the company collapsed into administration
story.summary: Cazoo, the online used-car retailer Alex Chesterman founded in 2018, listed in New York through a SPAC in August 2021 at a valuation of about $7 billion. In January 2023, after heavy losses, a retreat from mainland Europe and a 93 per cent share fall, Chesterman cut its targets, announced closures and job cuts and moved from chief executive to executive chairman; he left the board in December 2023. After 728 redundancies and a failed search for funding, Cazoo entered administration on 21 May 2024.
paragraphs: In August 2021, Alex Chesterman and his son rang the opening bell at the New York Stock Exchange. Cazoo, the online used-car retailer he had founded in London in 2018 and launched in December 2019, had just listed by merging with Ajax, a special purpose acquisition company backed by the investor Daniel Och. Most reports valued it at about $7 billion; City AM put it at $8 billion at the $10 listing price. Chesterman, who had earlier built LoveFilm and Zoopla, had talked of building "the Amazon of cars".

Seventeen months later the ground had shifted. In 2022 Cazoo reported a £243 million loss for the first half, withdrew from mainland Europe and cut about 750 jobs. Its shares had fallen about 93 per cent in a year and were trading near 21 cents, below the exchange's $1 minimum. Sales were still growing: more than £1.2 billion of revenue for 2022, and well over 100,000 cars sold online in Britain in three years.

On 18 January 2023 Chesterman announced a reset. Cazoo would aim for 40,000 to 50,000 UK cars that year, close more preparation and handover sites and cut more jobs, under what he called "more modest top line ambitions". From April he would step aside as chief executive to become executive chairman, handing day-to-day running to the operating chief, Paul Whitehead. He said the plan should carry Cazoo towards profit "without the need to raise further funding over the next 18-24 months."

It did not hold. In a debt-for-equity swap agreed in September and completed in early December 2023, about $630 million of debt was converted into $200 million, diluting shareholders further, and Chesterman left the board with four other directors. In March 2024 Cazoo said it would stop selling cars itself and become a marketplace; 728 people were made redundant between March and mid-May. On 1 May it said it had found no new funding, and on 21 May administrators from Teneo were appointed, keeping 208 staff for the time being. By then the shares had lost more than 99 per cent of their value.

quote.text: the man who is truly good and wise, we think, bears all the chances life becomingly and always makes the best of circumstances, as a good general makes the best military use of the army at his command and a good shoemaker makes the best shoes out of the hides that are given him
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: Aristotle's shoemaker works with the hides he is given, not the ones he hoped for. By January 2023 Cazoo's leaders were cutting a smaller plan from what was left. A few lines later Aristotle concedes that making the best of things cannot promise a good ending, and this story does not argue with him.

reflection: It is tempting to read a collapse backwards, as if the ending were obvious from the opening bell. It was not obvious to the people who took jobs at Cazoo, bought its shares or wrote its plans, and more than seven hundred of them lost their work in its last months. In January 2023 its leaders wrote a smaller, more careful plan, and even that was not enough.

Your plans have dates and assumptions in them too: when money will arrive, how many customers will sign, how long the savings last. You cannot make them certain. You can write beside each one the few things that must stay true for it to hold, and read that list on a rested morning rather than a frightened one.
invitation: Take one plan you are working to and write beside it the single assumption it depends on most. Put a reminder in your calendar a month from today to check whether that assumption still holds.

cross_checks.claim: Cazoo listed on the New York Stock Exchange through a SPAC in August 2021 at a valuation of about $7 billion (City AM: $8 billion at the listing price)
In 2022 Cazoo withdrew from mainland Europe and cut hundreds of jobs (about 750)
On 18 January 2023 Cazoo cut its targets and announced Chesterman would move from chief executive to executive chairman, with Paul Whitehead as CEO
In December 2023, after about $630 million of debt was converted to $200 million, Chesterman left the board with four other directors
After 728 redundancies, Teneo was appointed administrator on 21 May 2024 and kept 208 staff
By May 2024 Cazoo had lost more than 99 per cent of its value

research_notes: Valuation at listing differs by source and currency: about $7bn (MoneyWeek before the deal, Fortune, BusinessCloud, CarsVansandBikes), $8bn at the $10 listing price (City AM), about £5bn (PA, via The Irish News) and more than £6.3bn (Euronews). The story gives the common $7bn figure and City AM's $8bn. Share fall by January 2023: 93% over the past year (Sharecast; City AM via MarketScreener), about 98% from the February 2021 high of $14 (BusinessCloud), 97% in a Telegraph headline that could not be loaded; the story uses 93% in a year. Europe job cuts: City AM via MarketScreener gives 750; Sharecast says hundreds; the story says 'about 750'. Debt swap: City AM says it was agreed in September 2023; Car Dealer reports its completion in December, converting $630m into $200m. Chesterman's role in the collapse: he had left the board in December 2023, five months before the administration, and no public comment from him on the collapse was found, so the story does not give one. A line widely attributed to Chesterman in search summaries ('made mistakes along the way for sure but learnt a lot') is in fact from Paul Whitehead's March 2024 LinkedIn post, as quoted by BusinessCloud; it is not used. Blame: dealers and commentators quoted in Car Dealer and BusinessCloud give harsh views of Cazoo's model and of Chesterman's remarks about dealers; no court or regulator has assigned blame, so the story gives only facts and the company's and founder's own statements. Reports that Chesterman sold about £100m of shares in 2020 (The Times via The Negotiator; Car Dealer) are not used because they are not central to the episode. Funding is marked venture: Cazoo was backed by venture and growth investors before it listed through the SPAC.
